title: Thyroid, Adrenal & Pituitary Medications: Hormone Replacement, Suppression and Endocrine Emergencies
html:
Endocrine medications replace a missing hormone, suppress excess production, or modify a feedback pathway. Their effects often emerge over days to weeks, while an omitted dose, excessive dose, acute illness, or electrolyte shift can produce a rapid emergency. The RN must connect the medication to the gland, feedback loop, laboratory trend, cardiovascular status, fluid balance, and the client's ability to follow a precise regimen.

Learning goals

  • Administer levothyroxine consistently and recognize under- and over-replacement.
  • Monitor methimazole and propylthiouracil for agranulocytosis and liver injury.
  • Differentiate symptom control from correction of thyroid hormone production.
  • Use glucocorticoids and mineralocorticoids safely in adrenal insufficiency.
  • Prevent adrenal crisis during illness, surgery, vomiting, or abrupt steroid withdrawal.
  • Monitor desmopressin and other pituitary-directed therapies for serious adverse effects.

Think in feedback loops and time courses

Before giving an endocrine medication, identify the diagnosis, target hormone, whether treatment replaces or suppresses function, recent dose changes, expected time to effect, laboratory trend, interacting drugs, pregnancy status when relevant, and signs of crisis. Do not adjust long-term therapy from one nonspecific symptom or one isolated laboratory value without confirming the clinical context.

Replacement usually requires consistent dosing and surveillance. Suppressive therapy may produce delayed benefit because circulating hormone or downstream effects persist. Symptom-directed drugs may improve tachycardia or tremor without correcting the endocrine disorder. Teach clients which medication does which job.

Levothyroxine replaces thyroid hormone

Levothyroxine is synthetic T4 used to treat hypothyroidism. Give it consistently at the same time and in relation to food according to the prescription and product instructions—commonly on an empty stomach with water. Calcium, iron, some antacids, bile-acid sequestrants, tube feedings, and other products can reduce absorption; separate them by the prescribed interval rather than inventing a universal schedule.

Because the response is slow, thyroid studies are generally reassessed weeks after starting or changing a dose rather than hours later. Trend TSH and free T4 as appropriate to the cause of hypothyroidism; TSH alone may be misleading in central pituitary disease. Pregnancy, major weight change, malabsorption, interacting medications, and formulation changes may alter dose needs.

Levothyroxine is not a weight-loss drug
Excess thyroid hormone can cause life-threatening toxicity. Palpitations, tachycardia, angina, dysrhythmia, tremor, heat intolerance, insomnia, diarrhea, and unexplained weight loss suggest over-replacement and require review.

Protect the heart and identify adrenal risk

Older adults and clients with coronary disease may require cautious initiation and titration because thyroid hormone increases metabolic and cardiac demand. New chest pain, rapid dysrhythmia, or heart-failure symptoms after a dose change needs prompt assessment.

Unrecognized adrenal insufficiency can worsen when thyroid replacement accelerates metabolism. In a client with suspected or known adrenal insufficiency, glucocorticoid replacement may need to precede thyroid hormone according to the treatment plan. Never delay emergency treatment of adrenal crisis while waiting for routine endocrine testing.

Myxedema coma is severe decompensated hypothyroidism

Hypothermia, bradycardia, hypotension, hypoventilation, hyponatremia, hypoglycemia, and altered consciousness in severe hypothyroidism can indicate myxedema coma. Priorities include airway and ventilatory support, careful warming, glucose and electrolyte management, infection or other trigger evaluation, IV thyroid hormone and empiric glucocorticoid therapy as prescribed, and continuous cardiac monitoring. Oral home dosing is not adequate emergency treatment.

Antithyroid drugs suppress new hormone synthesis

Methimazole is commonly used for hyperthyroidism; propylthiouracil has more limited roles because of severe liver-injury risk, though it may be selected in specific situations such as early pregnancy or thyroid storm. These drugs reduce new hormone synthesis but do not instantly remove hormone already stored or circulating, so clinical improvement may take weeks.

Monitor thyroid studies and assess for rash, arthralgia, hypothyroidism, and medication-specific adverse effects. Pregnancy changes drug selection and dose goals; coordinate closely with endocrine and obstetric specialists. Radioactive iodine is not used during pregnancy or breastfeeding.

Fever or sore throat may signal agranulocytosis

Teach clients taking methimazole or propylthiouracil to stop the medication and contact the prescriber immediately for fever, chills, or persistent sore throat according to the treatment plan. Obtain a complete blood count with differential when ordered. Do not reassure the client that these symptoms are merely a viral illness until severe neutropenia has been considered.

Jaundice, dark urine, pale stool, pruritus, right-upper-quadrant discomfort, marked fatigue, or anorexia may indicate liver injury. Propylthiouracil carries a boxed warning for severe liver injury and acute liver failure. Stop and escalate according to the prescription and current guidance.

Beta blockers control symptoms, not hormone production

Beta blockers may reduce tachycardia, tremor, anxiety, and adrenergic symptoms while definitive therapy takes effect. Assess blood pressure, pulse, heart block, decompensated heart failure, asthma or bronchospasm risk, and masking of hypoglycemia. A lower heart rate does not prove that excess thyroid hormone has resolved.

Thyroid storm requires immediate multimodal treatment

High fever, severe tachycardia or dysrhythmia, agitation or delirium, vomiting or diarrhea, heart failure, and hepatic dysfunction in thyrotoxicosis suggest thyroid storm. Activate emergency care. Treatment may include a beta blocker, antithyroid drug, iodine given in the correct sequence after synthesis blockade, glucocorticoid, cooling, fluids, and treatment of the trigger. Avoid aspirin for fever because it can increase free thyroid hormone; use the prescribed alternative.

Glucocorticoids replace cortisol and suppress inflammation

Hydrocortisone or another glucocorticoid replaces cortisol in adrenal insufficiency. Higher stress dosing may be prescribed during fever, surgery, trauma, or serious illness. Clients should carry emergency identification and understand their written sick-day and injectable rescue plan. Vomiting or diarrhea that prevents oral medication requires urgent parenteral replacement and evaluation.

Glucocorticoids used for anti-inflammatory or immunosuppressive therapy can cause hyperglycemia, infection risk, mood and sleep change, hypertension, fluid retention, gastrointestinal injury, impaired wound healing, myopathy, skin changes, cataracts, glaucoma, and osteoporosis. Monitor by dose, duration, route, comorbidity, and concurrent therapy.

Do not stop chronic glucocorticoids abruptly
Prolonged or high-dose exposure can suppress the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis. Abrupt withdrawal may cause weakness, nausea, hypotension, hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, shock, and adrenal crisis. Follow the individualized taper.

Adrenal crisis is a shock emergency

Suspect adrenal crisis with hypotension or shock, severe weakness, abdominal symptoms, vomiting, dehydration, hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, or altered mental status—especially after steroid interruption, infection, surgery, trauma, or inability to retain medication. Draw ordered studies if this does not delay care, then give emergency IV glucocorticoid and isotonic saline with dextrose as prescribed. Monitor glucose, sodium, potassium, perfusion, urine output, rhythm, and the precipitating cause.

Fludrocortisone replaces mineralocorticoid activity

Primary adrenal insufficiency may require fludrocortisone to support sodium retention, potassium excretion, and intravascular volume. Monitor supine and standing blood pressure, weight, edema, sodium, potassium, symptoms of salt craving or dizziness, and renin when ordered. Hypertension, edema, hypokalemia, or rapid weight gain may signal excessive effect; persistent orthostasis or hyperkalemia may signal inadequate replacement or illness.

Desmopressin reduces free-water excretion

Desmopressin is an analog of antidiuretic hormone used for central diabetes insipidus and selected other indications. Verify the formulation, route, indication, dose, fluid plan, sodium, renal function, urine output, weight, thirst, and neurologic status. Products for nasal, oral, sublingual, or parenteral use are not interchangeable by volume or dose.

The major danger is water intoxication and hyponatremia. Headache, nausea, sudden weight gain, lethargy, confusion, muscle cramps, seizure, or falling sodium requires immediate assessment. Follow prescribed fluid restriction and sodium monitoring; during vomiting, diarrhea, fever, unusually high fluid intake, or other fluid-electrolyte disturbance, the plan may require holding the drug and contacting the prescriber.

Other pituitary-directed therapies

Somatropin replaces growth hormone in selected deficiencies. Monitor growth response, glucose, thyroid and adrenal function, intracranial-hypertension symptoms such as severe headache or visual change, edema, joint symptoms, and injection sites. It is not a general anti-aging or performance drug.

Octreotide suppresses growth hormone and several gastrointestinal hormones and may be used in acromegaly and other specialized conditions. Monitor glucose, heart rate, gastrointestinal effects, gallbladder disease, thyroid function during long-term therapy, and product-specific injection technique. Dopamine agonists such as cabergoline can reduce prolactin; assess orthostatic symptoms, nausea, impulse-control or neuropsychiatric effects, and cardiac monitoring requirements at higher cumulative exposure.

Apply clinical judgment

  1. Recognize cues: Identify the gland, replace-versus-suppress role, medication and formulation, dose timing, hormone and electrolyte trends, vital signs, fluid balance, illness, pregnancy, adherence, and interacting therapy.
  2. Analyze cues: Determine whether findings represent under-replacement, over-replacement, delayed treatment effect, adverse reaction, abrupt withdrawal, fluid imbalance, or endocrine crisis.
  3. Prioritize hypotheses: Adrenal crisis, thyroid storm, myxedema coma, agranulocytosis, acute liver injury, severe hyponatremia, dysrhythmia, and airway or circulatory compromise require urgent action.
  4. Generate solutions: Support airway and circulation, obtain time-sensitive labs without delaying care, replace deficient hormones, suppress excess production in the correct sequence, correct glucose and electrolytes, and treat the trigger.
  5. Take action: Administer the exact formulation consistently, stop and escalate suspected severe toxicity, provide stress dosing or rescue therapy as ordered, and teach sick-day and emergency plans.
  6. Evaluate outcomes: Reassess hemodynamics, mentation, temperature, rhythm, fluid balance, glucose, sodium, potassium, symptom trends, hormone studies, adherence, and return precautions.

Clinical example

A client with primary adrenal insufficiency has influenza, persistent vomiting, profound weakness, blood pressure 78/44 mm Hg, glucose 54 mg/dL, sodium 126 mEq/L, and potassium 5.9 mEq/L. The RN recognizes adrenal crisis rather than waiting for a routine clinic adjustment. The RN activates emergency response, supports airway and circulation, obtains ordered specimens without delaying therapy, administers IV hydrocortisone and isotonic fluid with dextrose according to protocol, monitors rhythm and electrolytes, and evaluates for infection. After stabilization, the client and caregiver repeat the sick-day and injectable rescue plan using teach-back.

Original educational synthesis. Endocrine diagnosis, hormone targets, medication selection, formulation, dosing, titration, tapering, pregnancy management, laboratory monitoring, sick-day plans, fluid restriction, and emergency treatment require current prescriptions, product labeling, institutional protocols, specialty and pharmacy resources, and qualified clinical supervision. This lesson is not medical advice, clinical decision support, continuing education, or an official NCSBN product.
